idiom_name: Handler wrapper forwarding to the primary and pushing a Marshal snapshot onto a bounded SizedQueue; ActiveSupport::Notifications as the Rails/ruby-kafka seam
implementation_notes: Core Ruby ships the thread-safe secondary channel but not the tap. Thread::Queue is a multi-producer, multi-consumer FIFO that 'implements all the required locking semantics', so the classic structure is a wrapper object: on each call it serializes an isolated snapshot of the message, enqueues it, and then invokes the original receiver with the untouched original; a dedicated analyzer Thread drains the queue. Thread model: every thread lives in one VM behind the GVL - MRI threads 'share a Ractor-wide global lock like GIL (GVL in MRI terminology), so they can't run in parallel' - the tap is therefore out-of-band in latency terms but only interleaved, not parallel: a CPU-bound analyzer still steals throughput from the primary handler, so push heavy analysis out of process. Copy point: never hand the live object down; Object#dup/#clone are documented shallow copies ('the instance variables of obj are copied, but not the objects they reference'), which aliases every nested Hash/Array, so the isolation point is Marshal.load(Marshal.dump(msg)) (or JSON/a snapshot method; Marshal refuses Proc, Method, Thread, IO/File/Socket and other system objects, anonymous classes/modules, and objects with singleton methods). Overflow policy must be explicit because Thread::Queue#push takes no capacity or non_block argument and never fails: use Thread::SizedQueue.new(max) and push(copy, true), whose non_block form raises ThreadError when full - rescue it and increment a visible drop counter (drop policy); the default SizedQueue push instead suspends the producer until space frees, feeding analyzer backpressure into the primary flow. Insert/remove: the wrapper is swapped at the handler boundary without touching sender or receiver. Inside Rails (and libraries like ruby-kafka, which is instrumented entirely through this seam) the idiomatic tap is ActiveSupport::Notifications.instrument('message.handled', payload) plus subscribe: subscribers receive name/duration/payload and the tap is removable with unsubscribe - but dispatch is synchronous in-band ('first executes the block and then notifies all subscribers once done'), so an offloading subscriber that just enqueues is the correct wire-tap shape. Prefer the queue wrapper for a real second channel; prefer Notifications when the payload should stay a plain object graph.
pitfalls: Thread::Queue is unbounded by design: its documented call sequence is push(object) with no capacity, timeout, or non_block option, so a stalled or crashed analyzer thread makes the tap a silent memory leak in the primary flow - pick a bound and a policy (drop, sample, or backpressure) deliberately and expose queue size/length as a metric.

Thread::SizedQueue's default push blocks the producer when full ('If there is no space left in the queue, waits until space becomes available'), which routes the analyzer's latency straight back into the message handler - use push(object, true) and rescue the documented ThreadError to drop-and-count instead of coupling the two flows.

dup and clone are documented shallow copies - 'the instance variables of obj are copied, but not the objects they reference' - so a tapped hash or struct still shares every nested object with the primary path and an analyzer's mutation corrupts the live message; the Marshal round-trip gives isolation but raises on Proc, Method, Thread, IO/File/Socket, anonymous classes and objects with singleton methods, so payloads carrying those need a JSON or hand-written snapshot.

ActiveSupport::Notifications runs subscribers synchronously once the instrumented block finishes, and it does NOT swallow subscriber crashes: Fanout collects them and re-raises the single exception, or an InstrumentationSubscriberError listing every class, inside the instrumented call - so an analyzer that raises fails the business message, and a slow subscriber delays it; offload work inside the subscriber.

On MRI the tap is never actually parallel: all threads share the one GVL ('Threads in a Ractor shares a Ractor-wide global lock like GIL (GVL in MRI terminology), so they can't run in parallel'), and Ruby 3's fiber scheduler does not change this - its hooks (io_wait, kernel_sleep, blocking_operation_wait, ...) only multiplex non-blocking fibers inside a thread, and a Thread::Queue instance stays in the single shared VM; a CPU-bound analyzer still preempts the primary handler, so true isolation means another process (or Ractor with shareable objects).
